title: 45% of Indian Exports to the US Escape New 10% Tariff as Commerce Ministry Points to Pharma and Smartphone Exemptions
excerpt: India says it secured a lower tariff rate than most countries under the US Section 301 forced-labour investigation, but textile exporters warn the new duties put them at a disadvantage against Asian rivals.
body:
• India's Commerce Ministry says 45% of Indian exports to the US — including generic pharmaceuticals, smartphones and products covered under Section 232 — will not face the new 10% tariff
  • The remaining 55% of exports will attract the additional 10% duty under the US Section 301 forced-labour investigation, on top of existing MFN tariffs
  • India's 10% rate is lower than the 12.5% originally proposed and places it in the lower tier among 60 affected economies
  • Textile exporters warn they face a disadvantage as Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia received quota exemptions that India did not

India Secures Lower Tier in US Tariff Overhaul

India has landed in the lower tier of a sweeping new US tariff regime, with the Commerce Ministry emphasising that nearly half of all Indian exports to the United States will remain untouched by the additional duties that took effect on Friday.

The Trump administration's final Section 301 measures, announced by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) on July 23, impose additional duties of 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 trading partners. The investigation, conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, alleges that these countries have failed to adequately enforce prohibitions on goods produced using forced labour.

India received a 10% rate — lower than the 12.5% proposed in June — which the Commerce Ministry attributed to "sustained engagement with the USTR through detailed written submissions, in-person consultations and participation in public hearings." The new levy applies on top of standard US most-favoured-nation tariffs.

What's Exempt, What's Not

The ministry's statement highlighted several significant exemptions. Generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones — two of India's fastest-growing export categories to the US — face no additional duty. Products already covered under the separate Section 232 tariffs, including steel, aluminium and auto parts (which carry duties of 25–50%), are also excluded from the new 10% levy.

On account of these exemptions, an estimated 45% of India's exports to the United States remain outside the scope of the additional tariff. The remaining 55% — encompassing engineering goods, chemicals, machinery, plastics, leather products, gems and jewellery, garments, furniture and most other manufactured goods — will now attract the extra 10% on top of existing duties.

The Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) estimated that roughly 70% of Indian exports by value will face the combined burden of MFN tariffs plus the new Section 301 duty, noting that about 8% of exports — those covered under Section 232 — already face tariffs of 25–50% and are not subject to additional charges.

Textiles: The Pain Point

The sharpest criticism has come from India's textile industry. The Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI) warned that the new measures put Indian exporters at a clear disadvantage against Asian competitors.

"The differential treatment risks diverting sourcing orders for textile and apparel items away from India."

— Ashwin Chandran, Chairman, Confederation of Indian Textile Industry

The issue: the final US measures include tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) that allow specified textile and apparel shipments from Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia — if produced using US-origin cotton and fibre — to enter the United States free of the Section 301 duty. India was excluded from this mechanism.

India's textile and apparel exports to the US, its largest market for the sector, are worth nearly $11 billion annually. Bangladesh exported about $8 billion in apparel to the US in 2024, with Indonesia and Cambodia shipping roughly $4 billion each. The textile-specific mechanism has not yet been operationalised, leaving its practical impact unclear, but exporters say the signal to sourcing managers is already negative.

Trade Talks Continue

Despite the new tariffs, India emphasised it remains committed to concluding a bilateral trade agreement with the United States. "The government remains committed to working with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement," the ministry said, adding that discussions on sector-specific issues, including textiles, would continue as part of broader negotiations.

The two countries have been negotiating a trade pact since last year. India and the US reached a framework for an interim reciprocal trade deal in February, but the final agreement remains elusive. The GTRI questioned whether the Section 301 measures were genuinely targeted at forced-labour concerns, arguing the tariff "appears to serve primarily as a mechanism to preserve the Trump administration's tariff wall after the expiry of the temporary Section 122 tariffs."

For Indian exporters, the calculus is straightforward: the new 10% duty will squeeze margins in competitive sectors and could accelerate sourcing shifts to countries with preferential access. The pharmaceutical and smartphone exemptions provide a buffer, but for manufacturers in chemicals, leather, engineering goods and especially textiles, the US market just became more expensive to serve.
nri_angle: The new tariff regime directly affects Indian businesses and diaspora entrepreneurs engaged in US-India trade, particularly in textiles, chemicals and manufactured goods.
